title: Symbolic-Permutation-Based Direct Sparse Jacobian Assembly for Accelerated Power-Flow Analysis
abstract: The repeated assembly of the sparse Jacobian matrix constitutes a primary computational bottleneck in the Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis. Through an algebraic equivariance analysis of the Jacobian matrix, this paper proposes a direct sparse Jacobian assembly method based on symbolic permutation. By pre-applying the permutation to the admittance matrix during a one-time symbolic phase, the runtime bus-type projection overhead is entirely eliminated. Consequently, complex Jacobian differentiation and global matrix assembly fuse into a single operation, yielding a single-pass, branchless algorithm that streams values directly into contiguous memory. The framework is realized in the open-source RustPower solver. Benchmarks on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate that the proposed assembly is 24.4-30.1x faster than the MATPOWER- style baseline and 6.0-7.8x faster than the Schafer-Braun optimized assembly. End-to-end, the grid-level solve time is 11.7x-154.3x faster than pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba, while leaving numerical results and convergence behavior unchanged. Compared with the native C++ LightSim2Grid 1.0.0, grid-level performance is comparable on IEEE 39 and 1.3x-1.8x faster on IEEE 118 and the PEGASE systems. The method extends directly to general problems where a sparse Jacobian inherits its structure from a static network operator, including transient stability analysis, EMT simulation, and OPF Hessian assembly.

[III-A Non-Holomorphic Deadlock and the Dual Real-Mapping Paradigm] Redundant Differentiation: Wasting significant CPU cycles and arithmetic throughput evaluating derivatives for dropped states (e.g., slack and PV bus voltage magnitudes) that are subsequently discarded. Indirect Spatial Partitioning: Relying on extensive layout-mapping tables to index and route derivatives into traditional $\bm{J}_{11}$ through $\bm{J}_{22}$ sub-blocks, introducing severe pointer-dereferencing and indirection overheads inside the iteration loop. Non-Contiguous Scatter Assembly: Enforcing dimensional reduction via scattered writes that distribute values across disjoint matrix segments, which completely disrupts hardware prefetching, invalidates CPU cache lines, and severely limits parallel scalability. These limitations transform the iteration hot path into a performance graveyard of branch mispredictions and cache invalidations, which also significantly lower the parallel efficiency on modern CPUs and GPUs.

LightSim2Grid uses a C++ backend on a pre-built model. Given the rapid evolution of power-flow software, comparisons are performed using fixed software releases. A: The work addresses the significant computational cost associated with Jacobian matrix assembly in iterative optimization algorithms. A novel approach is presented that leverages symbolic permutation and algebraic equivariance to streamline the process, eliminating runtime overhead and fusing differentiation and assembly steps. The resulting algorithm demonstrates substantial speedups compared to existing methods, achieving significant reductions in solve times across various benchmark power systems. The technique's applicability extends beyond power-flow analysis to other network-based optimization problems.
B: The work addresses the computational expense of Jacobian matrix assembly within Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis, a process that traditionally involves repeated calculations and inefficient memory access patterns. The authors propose a novel approach based on symbolic permutation, pre-applying topological transformations to the admittance matrix to eliminate runtime overhead and consolidate differentiation and assembly into a single pass. This results in a branchless algorithm that directly streams values into contiguous memory, achieving significant speedups over existing methods, including a 11.7x-154.3x improvement in grid-level solve time compared to pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba. The framework was implemented in RustPower and validated on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241.

title: Sustainable Cloud-Fog-Edge Systems for Smart Buildings: Algorithmic Adaptation under Memory Constraints and Dynamic Orchestration Strategies
abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.

Simple Block Processing: Iterative processing using fixed-size data buffers $W$ (e.g., 1024 lines). This simulates diversity by simply moving to a new block. Block Processing with Explicit Diversity Management (Proposed Method): This innovative strategy explicitly manages the buffer content to ensure diversity. The buffer is filled. The buffer is sorted (e.g., based on accMotion value), complexity $O(W\log W)$. Only samples at the extremities of the distribution (e.g., the lower and upper halves) are retained to maximize sample diversity. The resulting empty spaces are refilled with new data. The GHA step is executed on this diversified buffer.

[V-B K-MEANS Clustering for Activity Analysis] The differences between the results in C++ and Python programs can be attributed to several factors. The C++ program processes the data in blocks of 1024 rows, while the Python program processes the data sequentially. This may affect how the eigenvalues and eigenvectors are updated. The initial parameters, such as the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, may be initialized differently in the two programs, which may influence the final results. The C++ program uses an online approach to update the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, while the Python program uses a batch approach. This may lead to differences in the convergence of the results. The Python program ignores rows without payload, which can reduce the number of data rows processed, while the C++ program does not seem to have this logic. The C++ program normalizes the data by ignoring some columns (1, 3, and 6), while the Python program normalizes all columns. This can lead to differences in the values of the processed data.

[VI-A Inherent Limitations of the Proposed Methodology] We detail the disadvantages and limitations of the proposed approach, as required by the critiques (Critique 2): PCA Linearity Limit: PCA (and GHA) is a linear method. It can only capture linear relationships between variables. If data relationships are non-linear, this method may not capture the true structure. Information Loss: Dimensionality reduction entails an inevitable loss of total variance. Implementation and Performance Cost: The explicit memory management strategy (sorting) increases the implementation complexity and the time complexity to $O(W\log W)$ per iteration, which affects speed on low-power devices. Dependency on Sorting Criterion: The success of the diversity preservation method relies heavily on choosing the correct variable for sorting (e.g., accMotion). A poor choice could compromise the preservation of diversity. Ecosystem Compatibility: There is a recognized time lag in algorithm development between microcontroller ecosystems (ARDUINO and Micropython).
A: The work addresses the challenges of deploying machine learning algorithms within resource-constrained environments, specifically focusing on smart building applications. Researchers developed a system utilizing low-power microcontrollers and a lightweight orchestration framework to manage data acquisition, storage, and processing. They adapted the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm for Principal Component Analysis, employing a data buffering strategy with sorting to achieve comparable results to full-memory processing while mitigating memory limitations.
B: The study investigates a method for processing large datasets on resource-constrained microcontrollers within a smart building environment. To address limited memory, a novel block processing strategy was developed that explicitly manages data diversity by sorting buffer contents and retaining extreme samples, resulting in a time complexity of O(W log W) per iteration. Experimental validation using Tour Perret sensor data demonstrated that this approach achieves comparable results to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states. The work also acknowledges limitations, including the method's reliance on linear relationships and the performance impact of the sorting step.

title: Deep learning methods for stochastic Galerkin approximations of random domain problems
abstract: This work considers strong and weak stochastic Galerkin approximations of random domain problems for the elliptic random partial differential equation (PDE). The random domain problems are realized by sufficiently regular random domain mapping, allowing a transformation on deterministic reference domain. A traditional numerical method for solving the resulting high-dimensional coupled stochastic Galerkin systems is replaced by deep learning techniques. We compare a physics-informed neural network approach, based on the strong stochastic Galerkin residual, with a Deep Ritz approach, based on the weak stochastic Galerkin system, reformulated as Ritz energy minimization. The neural networks serve as surrogates for the deterministic spectral coefficients of the respective stochastic Galerkin solution. The stochastic parameters are not used as neural network input parameters and the stochastic domain is not sampled during training. The efficiency of the methods is demonstrated on a randomly stretched interval and a randomly deformed annulus in two spatial dimensions.

A: The study addresses the computational challenges arising from elliptic partial differential equations defined on domains that vary randomly. Researchers developed deep learning techniques to approximate the solutions of stochastic Galerkin approximations, replacing traditional methods for solving high-dimensional systems. Two approaches were investigated: a physics-informed neural network utilizing the strong stochastic Galerkin residual and a Deep Ritz method based on energy minimization, both serving as surrogates for deterministic spectral coefficients. Numerical experiments on geometric domains demonstrated the efficiency of these deep learning-based approximations.
B: The study addresses the solution of elliptic partial differential equations defined on domains that vary randomly. A stochastic Galerkin method is employed to transform the random problem into a system of high-dimensional equations, which are then approximated using deep learning techniques. Specifically, physics-informed neural networks and a Deep Ritz approach are compared, with the neural networks acting as surrogates for the deterministic coefficients within the Galerkin expansion. The methods were tested on a randomly stretched interval and a randomly deformed annulus in two spatial dimensions to demonstrate their efficiency.

title: Particle-Number-Preserving Quantum Signal Processing for Thermal Properties: Canonical-Ensemble Estimation and Grand-Canonical Reconstruction
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for estimating canonical thermal properties of particle-number-conserving second-quantized Hamiltonians using quantum simulations. The framework integrates initial state preparation with mixed Dicke states, particle-number-preserving Trotterized simulation, and generalized quantum signal processing to estimate canonical partition functions and observables. Building on this canonical scheme, we introduce a grand-canonical reconstruction scheme in which the same quantum measurement data can be reused for arbitrary chemical potentials through classical reweighting, thereby avoiding repeated quantum circuit executions as the chemical potential is varied. We prove the existence of system-size-independent temperature regimes in which both the canonical and reconstructed grand-canonical schemes have lower asymptotic time complexity than classical Lanczos methods, up to polynomial factors, for physically relevant Hamiltonians. We numerically validate our theoretical results for the two-dimensional Hubbard model in both weak- and intermediate-coupling regimes.

The authors propose a quantum simulation approach combining state preparation, Trotterization, and quantum signal processing to estimate partition functions and observables. Their method includes a reconstruction technique allowing for chemical potential variation without additional quantum computations, and they demonstrate its efficiency compared to classical Lanczos methods through numerical experiments on the Hubbard model.
B: The work introduces a quantum simulation framework for estimating thermal properties of systems with conserved particle number, leveraging quantum signal processing and mixed Dicke states. The algorithm first estimates canonical properties within specific particle sectors using Algorithm 1, then reconstructs grand-canonical properties through classical reweighting, avoiding repeated quantum circuit executions. Numerical validation was performed on the two-dimensional Hubbard model, demonstrating that the proposed approach can outperform classical Lanczos methods under certain conditions, with the relative error of the ground state energy affecting the circuit sampling complexity.

title: Metric-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Object Hallucination Reduction in LVLM-Based Image Captioning
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.

Section 4 presents the experimental results, and Section 5 reports the ablation studies. Section 6 provides discussions, while Section 7 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

There is a slight increase in SPICE, BLUE, and BERTScore, which we attribute to the generated captions being more factual, concise, and focused, resulting in shorter and more precise outputs. When ground truth captions are available, incorporating METEOR and BERTScore, as in Ours+, significantly improves caption quality. It is evident that Ours+ significantly improves captioning performance across SPICE, BLEU, and BERTScore, surpassing all previous baselines. Extend evaluations to more complex dataset: We evaluate our model on the Visual Genome dataset using the CCEval metric from Halle-switch [ 91 ] to assess its performance in more complex settings with denser object in the image.

[VII Limitations and Future Directions] While our framework effectively mitigates object hallucination, several limitations remain. First, OCS is currently defined over object sets and therefore primarily targets object-level hallucination. Hallucinations involving incorrect attributes (e.g., color) or relations (e.g., spatial or interaction errors) are not explicitly optimized. However, since OCS is fundamentally a precision–recall (F1-based) formulation, it can be extended to structured units such as (object, attribute) pairs or (subject, relation, object) triplets, provided reliable automatic extraction is available. Exploring such extensions is an important direction for future work. Second, in real-world deployment settings where ground-truth annotations are unavailable, hallucination mitigation depends on the coverage and accuracy of the object detector used to construct visual object sets. Detectors limited to fixed vocabularies (e.g., COCO’s 80 classes) may leave non-COCO hallucinations undetected. Integrating open-vocabulary detection models could further improve robustness in real-world applications.
A: The paper addresses the problem of object hallucination in image captioning models, specifically within Large Vision-Language Models. To mitigate this, the authors propose a reinforcement learning framework that utilizes natural language processing metrics, such as an Object Consistency Score and KL-regularization, to guide the fine-tuning of adapters on a frozen LVLM backbone. Experimental results on the COCO and Visual Genome datasets demonstrate a substantial reduction in hallucination, up to 41% and 29% respectively, while also maintaining or improving caption quality as measured by metrics like BERTScore and METEOR.
B: The study investigates a method for improving the accuracy of image captioning models, which sometimes fabricate objects not present in the image. Researchers developed a reinforcement learning approach that uses automated language metrics to guide the model's learning process, reducing the need for human intervention. This framework incorporates a novel consistency score and regularization techniques to prevent undesirable behaviors and improve training efficiency, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in hallucinated objects across multiple datasets. The findings suggest that models can be refined through automated feedback, potentially opening avenues for more scalable training methods.

title: Physics-informed random neural architectures on compact boundaryless multiply connected manifolds for random-operator models in machine learning and uncertainty quantification
abstract: We introduce stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) for stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators. The method enforces physics through a structural probabilistic coupling: a common Gaussian stochastic germ drives both the SBVP random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture. The stochastic neural network is non-feedforward and intrinsically random. A latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix, all governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. For deterministic inputs, the network output is random and can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training is performed in observation space: SBVP simulations produce random observables, while the SNN defines a predictive conditional probability density function. The supervised objective combines data fidelity, through negative log-likelihood, with a cross-entropy alignment term relative to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution. The resulting target is a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, with a dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model--data mismatch. The shared stochastic germ yields common-random-numbers Monte Carlo estimators and reduced-variance gradients. The method uses only evaluations of the SBVP solution mapping, without differentiating or modifying it, and avoids PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the approach in SBVP-consistent and SBVP-misspecified regimes. A generalized-posterior formulation is also outlined for hyperparameter inference and posterior averaging without per-query reoptimization.

Neuron locations and connectivity are determined by a latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact manifold, resulting in a sparse random weight matrix governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. B: This work addresses the challenge of solving stochastic boundary-value problems where the governing operators are themselves random. The authors propose a novel framework using stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) that incorporates randomness in both the operator and the network architecture, driven by a shared stochastic process. The network’s structure is defined by a latent Gaussian field and a Poisson point process on a manifold, resulting in a non-feedforward architecture with sparse connectivity and random weights, trained using a combination of data fidelity and distribution alignment.

title: Linear and entropy-stable scheme for the dynamic van der Waals model of non-isothermal liquid-vapor flows
abstract: In this paper, we propose a linear and decoupled fully discrete scheme that preserves the entropy production property for the dynamic van der Waals model. This model provides a thermodynamically consistent diffuse-interface framework for describing non-isothermal phase transitions in single-component liquid-vapor systems, containing the coupled conservation laws of mass, momentum and energy. We first introduce an equivalent reformulation of the governing equations that avoids the use of chain-rule identities, which generally fail under discrete differentiation. Further, a component-wise convex-splitting method is employed to calculate the discrete chemical potential and temperature. This treatment provides a discrete entropy-stable inequality without a time step restriction. Based on the explicitly treated velocity, the scheme allows the three conservation equations to be solved linearly and sequentially in a decoupled manner. Since the momentum equation does not directly affect the entropy-stability analysis, we use a classical linear semi-implicit scheme to solve it. Numerical experiments verify the expected numerical accuracy. Simulations of droplet evaporation and two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects further demonstrate the proposed method can capture complex non-isothermal phase-transition dynamics while numerically reproducing the discrete entropy production behavior.

A: The work addresses the numerical simulation of phase transitions in liquid-vapor systems using a dynamic van der Waals model, which incorporates conservation laws for mass, momentum, and energy. To improve stability and reduce physical scale differences, the governing equations are non-dimensionalized and reformulated to avoid issues with discrete differentiation, and a component-wise convex-splitting method is used to calculate the chemical potential and temperature. The resulting scheme demonstrates first-order temporal accuracy and second-order spatial accuracy, as verified through convergence tests on a domain with dimensions 100x100, and successfully simulates phenomena like droplet evaporation and Leidenfrost effects.
B: The study addresses the simulation of phase transitions in fluids by developing a numerical scheme for a specific thermodynamic model. Researchers reformulated governing equations and utilized a convex-splitting method to ensure entropy stability during discretization, avoiding issues with discrete differentiation. The resulting scheme allows for a decoupled, linear solution of conservation equations, with a classical approach used for the momentum equation. Validation through simulations of droplet evaporation and Leidenfrost effects demonstrates the scheme's ability to capture complex dynamics while maintaining numerical stability.

title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
abstract: Multi-domain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) flexibly model medium-specific representations to solve fluid--solid conjugate heat transfer (CHT). However, standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports, which can yield plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures. We propose Cova-PINN, a multi-domain PINN framework that aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. Cova-PINN jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. We evaluate Cova-PINN on four triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers and a geometrically distinct DualMS design against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented, and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol. Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors across the four TPMS topologies by $37.7\%$ and $60.2\%$, respectively, while also improving full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS.

The researchers developed a novel physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework, termed Cova-PINN, which integrates conservation principles across different domains and scales. Through joint optimization of local balances and global closure conditions, the method achieves significant improvements in outlet temperature and energy transfer accuracy compared to existing PINN approaches. Experimental validation on various heat exchanger designs demonstrates the enhanced performance of Cova-PINN.
B: The study addresses challenges in modeling fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer within complex geometries, where existing multi-domain neural network approaches struggle with accurate energy transfer. Researchers developed Cova-PINN, a framework that aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths and jointly optimizes local balances and global closure conditions. Evaluations on four triply periodic minimal surface heat exchangers and a DualMS design demonstrated that Cova-PINN reduced average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors by 37.7% and 60.2%, respectively, compared to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT. The method employs a two-stage training process, initially fixing flow networks and subsequently updating thermal parameters while retaining standard energy equations and interface conditions.

title: PINNs for N=2* holography
abstract: Can a holographic theory be reconstructed from its equation of state? We investigate this question using physics-informed neural networks in the bosonic-mass sector of the Pilch--Warner model. We first validate the PINN approach against an analytic solution encoding the leading high-temperature corrections to the conformal equation of state. We then reconstruct nonlinear black-brane geometries and the scalar potential using thermodynamics, ultraviolet asymptotics, Ward identities, and horizon regularity. Independent solutions of the bulk Einstein-scalar equations demonstrate that accurately reproducing thermodynamics with a trained PINN does not guarantee an accurate reconstruction of the scalar potential. High-precision knowledge of the high-temperature equation of state constrains nonlinear interactions in the bulk scalar potential. Fixing the cubic coupling to its exact PW value, motivated by this high-temperature extraction, reduces the maximum sampled error in the reconstructed scalar self-interactions by a factor of $\sim 15$ compared with constraining only the bulk scalar mass. Adding knowledge of the bulk viscosity of the gauge theory plasma further reduces this error by an additional factor of $\sim 13$, with independent forward solutions reproducing the bulk viscosity within $0.09\%$.

B: The study explores the potential of using machine learning techniques to derive physical systems from thermodynamic constraints. Researchers employed a neural network architecture trained to satisfy governing equations and validated it against a known analytical solution. The investigation then focused on reconstructing geometric properties and potential energy functions, revealing that thermodynamic accuracy does not always translate to accurate reconstruction of all physical parameters. Incorporating additional constraints, such as viscosity, significantly improved the precision of the reconstructed parameters.

title: A structure-preserving neural density functional for the ions of a polymer electrolyte
abstract: Predicting the structure and response of inhomogeneous polymer electrolytes requires a description of ion correlations that retains molecular-scale accuracy while remaining transferable across spatial scales and geometries. We develop a neural density functional for electrolytes that preserves spatial symmetries, thermodynamic integrability and the Noether identities, with perfect screening recovered in stable, noncritical bulk states. Its nonlinear density dependence captures the concentration-dependent correlations missed by a pair closure, including a crossover from enhanced to suppressed long-wavelength number fluctuations at strong coupling. The functional describes density profiles at an untrained salt concentration and predicts bulk structure factors and the long-wavelength number response. Trained solely on planar density and internal-force profiles from molecular dynamics, the functional predicts ionic structure in larger domains and in two-dimensional external fields. On the same ion data, it is more accurate than three other neural density-functional architectures and keeps its accuracy with a quarter of the training runs, where the errors of the best alternative grow by about two thirds. The spatial transferability provides a necessary foundation for connecting molecular correlations to continuum predictions at larger scales.

A: The study addresses the challenge of accurately modeling the behavior of ionic systems within a specific material context, aiming for a balance between detailed molecular information and broader applicability. A novel neural density functional is constructed, incorporating physical constraints to ensure consistency with known laws and symmetries. The resulting functional demonstrates improved predictive capabilities compared to existing methods, particularly in capturing complex correlations and transferring spatial information, and requires significantly less training data. This approach seeks to bridge the gap between atomistic simulations and macroscopic continuum models.
B: The work addresses the development of a neural density functional to model the behavior of electrolytes, focusing on preserving key physical symmetries and thermodynamic properties. The functional is trained using force matching, weighting bins inversely proportional to the variance of molecular dynamics estimates and compensating for a suppression factor in the force density. The resulting functional demonstrates improved accuracy compared to alternative architectures, achieving errors of 1.50% and 3.11% for ion profiles at specific dielectric constants, and maintains this accuracy even when trained on only a quarter of the available data.

title: A Relaxed Maximum-Based Normal \texorpdfstring{$S$}{S}-Iteration Method for Generalized Absolute Value Equations
abstract: A relaxed maximum-based normal $S$-iteration method (RMNSI) is proposed for solving generalized absolute value equations (GAVEs). The method combines a maximum-based fixed-point formulation with a constant relaxation parameter and avoids the selection of an auxiliary matrix. Assuming that $A+B$ is non-singular, both stages require linear systems with the same coefficient matrix $A+B$, allowing a single factorization to be reused throughout the iteration. A single spectral condition is established that guarantees unique solvability of the GAVE and global convergence from an arbitrary initial vector. An admissible range of the relaxation parameter is characterized, and $R$-linear convergence and error estimates are derived. Since the global condition can be conservative, a local convergence analysis based on the solution sign pattern is also presented. Numerical experiments on complementarity-derived, dense mixed-sign, and asymmetric ridge-regression problems are presented, and comparisons with several recent methods demonstrate the competitive efficiency and accuracy of RMNSI. The results further indicate that the preferred relaxation parameter depends mainly on the matrix structure and diagonal shift, while its dependence on the problem dimension is generally weak.
excerpts: [1 Introduction] Bringing these ideas together, we propose the relaxed maximum-based normal $S$ -iteration method, abbreviated as RMNSI. By setting $\Omega=O_{n}$, the auxiliary matrix is removed from the maximum-based formulation. The resulting fixed-point operator is evaluated first at the current iterate and then at a relaxed intermediate point. A constant parameter $\theta\geq 0$ controls this intermediate update and permits both under-relaxed and over-relaxed choices. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: The normal $S$ -iteration process is used within the maximum-based fixed-point framework to construct RMNSI without requiring the selection of an auxiliary matrix. Both stages require linear systems with the same coefficient matrix $A+B$; therefore, a single factorization can be computed once and reused throughout the iteration.

A: The paper introduces a relaxed maximum-based normal $S$-iteration method (RMNSI) designed to solve generalized absolute value equations, which avoids the need to select an auxiliary matrix by incorporating a constant relaxation parameter. The method utilizes a fixed-point operator evaluated at both the current iterate and a relaxed intermediate point, requiring linear systems with the same coefficient matrix $A+B$ to allow for a single factorization. Numerical experiments were conducted on complementarity-derived, dense mixed-sign, and asymmetric ridge-regression problems, demonstrating the method’s competitive efficiency and accuracy compared to several existing approaches.
B: The study addresses the solution of generalized absolute value equations, a class of nonlinear problems arising in various applications. A new iterative method, termed the relaxed maximum-based normal $S$-iteration method, is developed to improve computational efficiency and convergence properties. The approach incorporates a relaxation parameter and avoids the need for auxiliary matrices, streamlining the iterative process and reducing computational cost. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness and accuracy compared to existing techniques, highlighting its sensitivity to matrix structure and diagonal shift.

title: Numerical simulation of biological capsules based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes
abstract: In this work we introduce a numerical framework for the simulation of biological capsules based on meshes that adapt iteration-wise to the shape of the membrane. The discretization leverages a Hybrid High Order method (HHO) to solve a Stokes problem with a source term distributed on the interface between the internal and the external phases. The HHO discretization supports meshes composed of general polygons, permitting to use fitted meshes that can be easily generated by cutting the elements intersected by the interface. Moreover, polygonal meshes allow arbitrarily accurate interface discretizations without introducing bulk degrees of freedom. The presentation of the simulation algorithm is completed with a proof-of-concept numerical test on a well-established benchmark: the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow.

[Conclusion and Perspectives] In this work, we have proposed a novel approach for the simulation of capsule dynamics based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes, summarized in Algorithm 1. The methodology leverages a Hybrid High Order discretization for flow equations supporting polygonal meshes. The flexibility of the method in terms of mesh requirements allows to treat in a straightforward way the interface conditions associated to the fluid-structure interaction while keeping the overhead linked to mesh adaptation moderate. As a proof of concept, the performance of the polygonal interface-fitted approach has been tested successfully on a simple yet paradigmatic benchmark featuring a capsule undergoing moderate to strong deformation in shear flow.
A: The work addresses the simulation of deformable objects by adapting a mesh to the object's boundary. A Hybrid High Order (HHO) method is used to solve a Stokes problem on a mesh composed of general polygons, allowing for accurate interface discretization and easy mesh generation. The approach was validated through a test case involving the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow, demonstrating accurate reproduction of the capsule's trajectory and achieving results comparable to existing methods.
B: The study addresses the computational modeling of deformable objects with distinct internal and external phases. A novel numerical method, termed Hybrid High Order (HHO), is employed to solve a fluid dynamics problem, with the interface between the phases represented by a polygonal mesh that dynamically adjusts during the simulation. This approach facilitates accurate representation of the interface without unnecessary computational overhead in the bulk fluid domain, demonstrated through a benchmark test involving capsule deformation.

title: Mesh-Free Numerical Approximation of the Biharmonic Equation via Optimized Kolmogorov--Arnold Neural Networks
abstract: A mesh-free numerical framework based on \textit{Kolmogorov--Arnold Physics-Informed Neural Networks} (KAN-PINNs) is developed for the approximation of fourth-order elliptic boundary value problems, with specific application to the biharmonic equation governing thin plate deflection. Unlike conventional Multi-Layer Perceptrons relying on fixed nodal activations, learnable univariate functions parameterized via radial basis functions are deployed on network edges, while high-order differentiability is preserved through hyperbolic tangent activation mappings. The severe numerical stiffness inherent to fourth-order differential operators and fully clamped boundary conditions is addressed through a direct normalized residual formulation coupled with a hybrid, multi-stage AdamW-to-L-BFGS optimization pipeline. An automated \textit{24/7 hill-climbing search protocol} is implemented to systematically calibrate boundary penalty weights and optimization schedules. When evaluated on a smooth manufactured benchmark on the unit square, an error reduction factor exceeding $150\times$ is attained over successive iterations, culminating in a final relative $L_2$ error of $1.593 \times 10^{-5}$ ($0.00159\%$) and a training loss of $3.065 \times 10^{-6}$ utilizing only $7,801$ trainable parameters. These results demonstrate that high-order PDE problems can be accurately resolved using compact, mesh-free KAN-PINNs architecture without requiring auxiliary variable transformations or discrete mesh generation.
excerpts: [1 Introduction] The development of neural PDE solvers has also revealed important limitations associated with the optimization of physics-informed loss functions. In particular, Wang et al. [ 26 ] investigated gradient-flow pathologies in PINNs and demonstrated that the different components of the loss function can produce highly unbalanced optimization dynamics. Such behavior can make training difficult, particularly when differential operators introduce disparate spatial scales or higher-order differentiability requirements. Krishnapriyan et al. [ 11 ] further demonstrated that PINN formulations can exhibit failure modes for challenging PDEs, showing that the difficulties are not necessarily caused by insufficient neural-network expressivity but can instead arise from the structure and optimization of the physics-informed objective. For higher-order problems like the biharmonic equation, these optimization hurdles are amplified due to the repeated differentiation of network parameters. Consequently, recent studies have explored specialized PINN architectures and training strategies specifically tailored for fourth-order systems [ 7, 23, 12, 17 ].

[1 Introduction] Alternative neural formulations have also been established to address these optimization dynamics. The Deep Ritz method proposed by E and Yu [ 8 ] represents the solution using a neural network and minimizes the corresponding variational or energy functional rather than pointwise differential residuals. This approach establishes a direct connection between variational numerical methods and neural-network approximation. Similarly, the framework of Galerkin Neural Networks developed by Ainsworth and Dong [ 1 ] constructs finite-dimensional approximation spaces whose basis functions are generated by neural networks and subsequently uses these spaces within a Galerkin formulation, preserving classical error-control concepts while maintaining neural flexibility.

[5.4 Error reduction via automated exploration] Throughout the automated $24/7$ hill-climbing search comprising $124$ total training attempts, the algorithm successfully captured $19$ successive performance improvements. The automated train-change-improve loop systematically drove the error down from an initial baseline of $0.24\%$ to a final relative $L_{2}$ error of $0.00159\%$ ( $1.593\times 10^{-5}$), representing an overall error reduction factor exceeding $150\times$. Figure 5 illustrates this multi-step convergence trajectory across the successive new best models. As highlighted by the search trajectory, the decisive levers governing this high degree of convergence were the escalating, restarted L-BFGS polish schedule and the implementation of a strong Dirichlet boundary penalty weight ( $\lambda_{\text{dir}}=480$), which effectively controlled the severe numerical stiffness associated with the fourth-order biharmonic operator boundaries. Conversely, tests involving larger network widths, double-precision ( float64), and increased collocation sampling densities yielded negligible performance gains, confirming that optimization dynamics—rather than over-parameterization—dominate fourth-order PINN training.
A: This work introduces a novel neural network architecture, KAN-PINNs, to solve fourth-order elliptic partial differential equations, exemplified by the biharmonic equation. The method replaces standard activation functions with learnable radial basis functions along network edges, maintaining high-order differentiability and employing a sophisticated optimization strategy to handle numerical stiffness. The resulting model achieves a substantial reduction in error on a benchmark problem, demonstrating the potential for accurate solutions with a relatively small number of parameters and without traditional meshing techniques.
B: The work introduces a novel mesh-free numerical method, termed KAN-PINNs, for solving fourth-order elliptic boundary value problems, specifically the biharmonic equation. The approach utilizes radial basis functions on network edges and hyperbolic tangent activations to maintain high-order differentiability, addressing the challenges posed by the stiffness of fourth-order operators and clamped boundary conditions. Through a direct residual formulation and a hybrid AdamW-to-L-BFGS optimization pipeline, coupled with an automated hill-climbing search, the method achieved a relative $L_2$ error of $1.593 \times 10^{-5}$ on a manufactured benchmark, demonstrating a $150\times$ error reduction. The study emphasizes that optimization dynamics, rather than network size, are the dominant factor in training fourth-order PINNs.

title: A mesh-based neural energy method for the simulation of heterogeneous composites
abstract: Modeling heterogeneous materials remains a challenge for physics-informed neural networks such as the deep energy method (DEM). The DEM and its variants, here collectively referred to as the neural energy method (NEM), offer a differentiable variational framework. However, their conventional collocation-based implementation (C-NEM) often suffers from physically inadmissible displacement oscillations, integration errors, and high computational costs from automatic differentiation. This work introduces the mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM), extending the NEM through a mesh-based discretization of the displacement field. By interpolating nodal displacements via shape functions, the M-NEM imposes a kinematic constraint that suppresses oscillations. Furthermore, the method replaces automatic differentiation with algebraic shape function derivatives for strain computation and employs high-order Gaussian quadrature for accurate energy integration. On a directly comparable benchmark problem, the M-NEM reduces stress errors by up to three orders of magnitude relative to the C-NEM while being one to two orders of magnitude faster. On two further benchmarks involving extreme stiffness contrasts, only the M-NEM converges. A comparative study of neural architectures reveals that radial basis function neural networks (RBFNNs) yield optimal performance within the M-NEM, resolving sharp gradients at material interfaces with higher accuracy than multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with random Fourier feature (RFF) mapping and faster convergence than Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs).
excerpts: [1 Introduction] To address these issues, the current work proposes the mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM), extending the NEM through a mesh-based discretization. Shape-function interpolation, algebraic derivatives, and element-level Gaussian quadrature address the first three challenges. The fourth challenge of spectral bias is addressed by investigating the efficacy of alternative network architectures within this framework in a comparative study of MLPs with RFF mapping, KANs, and RBFNNs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the continuum mechanics foundation, the general NEM formulation, and the examined neural network architectures. Section 3 presents the methodology of the M-NEM and details how mesh-based discretization benefits the training process. Section 4 validates the approach through benchmark problems involving stiff inclusions and real-world material composites. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the findings and discusses future directions.

[2.2 Network implementation and optimization] In the conventional implementation, referred to in the current work as the C-NEM, the energy functional is evaluated on a set of collocation points and the deformation gradient is computed via automatic differentiation. This introduces three limitations that become critical for the simulation of heterogeneous composites. A sufficiently expressive network may produce physically inadmissible displacement oscillations between collocation points that remain invisible to the loss function as they do not affect the energy evaluated at the sampling locations, a phenomenon here referred to as geometric overfitting. Furthermore, computing the deformation gradient via automatic differentiation grows the computational graph with network depth and the number of integration points, increasing memory consumption and sensitivity to floating point precision. Finally, stochastic or low-order integration schemes introduce aliasing errors when the strain energy density varies abruptly across material interfaces.

A: The work addresses challenges in simulating heterogeneous materials using a neural energy method (NEM) framework, specifically focusing on issues arising from conventional collocation-based implementations. To overcome these limitations, the authors introduce a mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM) which employs shape function interpolation for displacement fields and algebraic derivatives for strain computation, alongside high-order Gaussian quadrature for energy integration. Benchmarking against a comparable method revealed stress errors reduced by up to three orders of magnitude and a speedup of one to two orders of magnitude, with radial basis function neural networks (RBFNNs) demonstrating superior performance and convergence compared to multi-layer perceptrons and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks. The study highlights the benefits of RBFNNs, which achieved a high-fidelity solution more than ten times faster than KANs on a carbon fiber reinforced polymer benchmark.
B: The study addresses limitations in existing neural energy methods for simulating complex material behavior. Researchers developed a mesh-based approach, termed M-NEM, to overcome issues like displacement oscillations and computational inefficiency found in traditional implementations. The method incorporates shape functions for kinematic constraints and utilizes algebraic derivatives and Gaussian quadrature to improve accuracy and speed. Results demonstrate significant reductions in stress errors and computational time compared to conventional methods, alongside improved convergence for materials with extreme stiffness contrasts.

title: Using Context Is Not Enough: Test-Time Training for Personalized Reward Modeling
abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models (LLMs) with human preferences, yet most pipelines learn a single reward model that overlooks individual differences in preferences. Personalized reward models (PRMs) address this by conditioning rewards on user-specific feedback, most commonly through in-context learning (ICL), where a user's historical comparisons are supplied as contextual preference pairs. However, we identify a key limitation of ICL-based PRMs: they fail to capture the preference relations conveyed by contextual pairs. To address this, we propose Preference-Aligned Test-Time Training (P-TTT), which explicitly encodes these relations into user-specific fast weights for personalized reward prediction. P-TTT introduces sequence-level update and apply operations to match the response-level granularity of preference feedback, together with a preference-aligned objective that directly uses pairwise preference relations to guide fast-weight adaptation. Notably, P-TTT is simple to implement and computationally efficient, updating fast weights within a single forward pass without inference-time backpropagation. Extensive experiments show that P-TTT more effectively captures historical preference relations and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.
excerpts: [1 Introduction] We propose Preference-Aligned Test-Time Training (P-TTT), a novel strategy for personalized reward modeling that enhances the model’s ability to capture preference relations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that P-TTT effectively captures preference relations and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

[3 Empirical Analysis] These results reveal a notable discrepancy: ICL-based PRMs can use contextual examples for prediction, yet struggle to capture the preference relations expressed in them. This suggests that simply placing preference pairs in the context as model input may be insufficient for models to reliably identify the their relations. In particular, the critical preference labels ( chosen or rejected) may not be effectively associated with the corresponding responses, especially when they are embedded in lengthy contextual examples. As a result, rather than modeling the preference relations themselves, models may rely on more readily accessible shortcut cues in historical prompts or responses, such as previously asked questions, to make predictions. Such reliance may limit model generalization to new target samples. We also explored simple prompting strategies to mitigate this issue (see the appendix E), but observed no improvement, suggesting that the difficulty may reflect an intrinsic limitation of how ICL captures preference relations. These findings motivate us to develop a method that strengthens the preference modeling capability of PRMs.

Among ICL-based methods, ICL’s weaker performance is consistent with our analysis in Section 3: its difficulty in capturing preference relations limits its ability to infer user interests and generalize effectively. Although PLUS learns a summarizer, compressing feedback into textual summaries may still discard fine-grained preference information. Embedding-based methods also offer limited gains over BTL, potentially due to information loss when encoding complex users’ histories into compact representations. MRM benefits from meta-learned adaptation, but constraining adaptation to low-dimensional combinations of shared reward functions may limit its ability to capture complex preferences patterns. Finally, the poor performance of In-Place TTT is consistent with the mismatch between its language modeling aligned objective and the goal of PRMs.

Existing approaches often rely on providing user history as context, but this method struggles to fully utilize the information contained within those historical comparisons. The researchers introduce a novel technique, Preference-Aligned Test-Time Training (P-TTT), which directly incorporates pairwise preference relations into the reward model's parameters during inference, resulting in improved personalization and performance over existing methods. This approach is designed to be computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass for weight updates.
B: The study investigates limitations in current personalized reward modeling approaches for aligning language models with user preferences, specifically highlighting the inability of in-context learning to effectively capture the relationships within preference pairs. To address this, the authors introduce Preference-Aligned Test-Time Training (P-TTT), a method that directly encodes these preference relations into user-specific fast weights through sequence-level updates and a preference-aligned objective. Experiments using three datasets and two model backbones demonstrated that P-TTT significantly outperformed existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 3.94 percentage points.

A sequential training approach is implemented, releasing gradients for inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances in a specific order determined by sensitivity analysis. A novel architecture, termed a sequential learning-based PINN, is developed to iteratively estimate inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances. The method employs a staged release of gradients, guided by sensitivity analysis, to improve the convergence and accuracy of the parameter estimation process. Results demonstrate a significant improvement in estimation accuracy and training speed compared to a conventional simultaneous training approach, validated through a comprehensive parameter perturbation analysis.

title: RMB: Reward Model Boosting Mitigates Reward Hacking
abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a powerful technique for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preference. However, it often suffers from the reward hacking issue, where policy optimization improves the proxy reward model while actually degrading performance with respect to the true human preference, due to the imperfection of the proxy. To address this, we propose Reward Model Boosting (RMB), a novel approach that enhances the robustness and reliability of the reward signal for RLHF. RMB first trains a set of reward models with a diversity-promoting regularizer. This encourages each model to learn complementary aspects of the reward landscape. Then, RMB learns a lightweight aggregator in the principle of boosting to aggregate the outputs of the diverse reward models into a more accurate and robust reward signal. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that RMB significantly improves reward accuracy on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, substantially mitigating the reward hacking issue and ultimately improving RLHF performance.

One possible explanation is that the training data do not contain sufficiently rich and independent learning signals: as more reward models are added, they increasingly learn redundant preference patterns, limiting the benefits of diversity regularization and boosting. Evaluating RMB on larger, higher-quality, and more diverse preference corpora is therefore an important direction for future work.
A: The study investigates a common challenge in training language models to align with human preferences: the tendency for optimization to exploit imperfections in the reward signal. Researchers developed a method called Reward Model Boosting (RMB) that involves training multiple reward models with a diversity-promoting technique and then combining their outputs using a boosting approach. Empirical evaluations across various datasets showed that RMB significantly improved reward accuracy and reduced the likelihood of reward hacking, leading to enhanced overall performance.
B: The study investigates a problem arising in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) where optimizing a proxy reward model can lead to undesirable outcomes. To address this, the authors introduce Reward Model Boosting (RMB), a technique that trains multiple reward models with a diversity-promoting regularizer and then aggregates their outputs using a lightweight aggregator. Experiments using a boosting approach that iteratively refines the reward model aggregator demonstrate significant improvements in reward accuracy and mitigation of reward hacking, with the aggregator adding minimal overhead to the reward model inference, averaging only 0.000088 of the base reward model pass.

title: Provable Method of Moments for Cryo-EM
abstract: We study the recovery of a three-dimensional volume in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) from noisy tomographic projections acquired at unknown viewing rotations, drawn independently and uniformly from $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. We show that, in a spherical-shell representation satisfying an explicit shell-separation condition, the first three moments generically determine the underlying real volume up to its intrinsic global $\mathrm{O}(3)$ ambiguity. The proof is constructive and yields a frequency-marching procedure that successively recovers the volume. Consequently, consistent recovery in the high-noise regime has sample complexity $n=ω(σ^6)$, where $n$ is the number of observations and $σ^2$ is the noise variance. Numerical experiments validate the constructive recovery scheme under finite sampling and additive noise, and indicate that direct third-moment optimization can succeed beyond the structural assumptions required by the constructive proof.

A: The work addresses the problem of reconstructing a three-dimensional volume from noisy projections, where the projections are acquired at unknown rotations. A constructive recovery scheme is developed based on the first three moments in a spherical-shell representation, which recovers the volume up to an ambiguity. Numerical validation using synthetic volumes, such as TRPV1 and the 80S ribosome, demonstrates the effectiveness of the method, with forward-marched shells exhibiting a relative error of $1.39\times 10^{3}$ at $\ell=2$ and backfilled shells reaching $2.07\times 10^{8}$. The experiments also suggest favorable optimization behavior, with aligned errors agreeing to within $10^{-6}$ for the 80S ribosome at signal-to-noise ratios greater than or equal to 1.
B: The work addresses the reconstruction of a 3D volume from projections subject to rotational uncertainty and noise. A theoretical framework is developed based on the analysis of moments in a specific representation, demonstrating a relationship between these moments and the underlying volume. The authors provide a constructive recovery algorithm and derive a sample complexity bound dependent on the noise variance, which is then verified through numerical simulations.

title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
abstract: Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.

title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.
